newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus oil crisis eases but Russia problems stay.
newsitem.headline: Belarus oil crisis eases but Russia problems stay.

text.p: An oil crisis in the former Soviet republic of Belarus, heavily dependent on Moscow for supplies, has eased but is not over yet, an official said on Tuesday.
Supplies to two big refineries, which almost ground to a halt last month, had somewhat resumed, said an official at state oil concern Belnefteprodukt who asked not to be named.
"Now we are refining 20,000 tonnes a day, but we refine 35,000 to 40,000 tonnes of oil when we are working normally," the official told Reuters.
He said that Russia would deliver about 500,000 tonnes of crude oil in January -- or about 50 percent of the monthly norm.

He blamed the problem partly on rules governing conversion of the country's rouble currency, fixed earlier this month in a floating corridor of 15,500-21,000 at a time when it traded freely on the interbank market at 25,000-27,000 per dollar.

Another problem was that LUKoil -- which, with two other Russian oil companies, Slavneft and YUKOS, heavily controls supplies to Belarus -- was demanding that Minsk privatise one of its two large refineries, at Novopolotsk.
LUKoil sent an official letter in December refusing to go along with a Russian-Belarussian oil supply deal until privatisation had been carried out at the plant.
The Statistics Ministry said on Tuesday that the plants refined 12.4 million tonnes of oil last year from 13.1 million in 1995 -- well below their combined capacity of about 40 million tonnes.
First Deputy Prime Minister Pyotr Prokopovych told a news conference late on Monday that a privatisation project for Novopolotsk was being prepared.
"Any investor can buy its shares but for us the main thing is not privatisation but attracting $350-$450 million to reconstruct the factory," he said.
Prokopovych said the Russian government, which sells oil to Belarus under a special quota deal struck last year, would have to solve the supplies problem.
But the Belnefteprodukt official said: "Neither Belarus nor Russia can force the companies to deliver oil. The only way out is to liberalise the oil market."
President Alexander Lukashenko, one of whose political goals is to form a union with Russia, has decreed that only six out of 60 domestic and Russian suppliers can sell oil to Belarus.
Oil prices in Belarus have come closer to world levels and are $105 a tonne from $94 in December, when supplies almost dried up and the republic was refining just 5,000-10,000 tonnes a day.
Belarus, with 1.39 million tonnes of domestic oil output, imports 10 million tonnes of Russian oil a year for its own needs, while it refines six million tonnes for Russia.
